text: Classification needs actual tiers to sort data into. Most organizations land on some version of the same small scheme — here's the common pattern, and where it varies.

Four tiers show up again and again: Public — fine for anyone to see. Internal — for employees, not damaging if it leaked. Confidential — real harm if disclosed, like customer records. Restricted, or Highly Confidential — the most sensitive tier, where a leak causes severe harm.

The label is just a name. What makes it meaningful is three questions: who can access it, what happens if it leaks, and what controls apply. Public needs none of that; Restricted needs the strictest controls the organization has — multi-factor authentication, tightly scoped access, mandatory audit trails.

Exact names and tier counts vary — three tiers, five tiers, different labels — and that's fine, as long as they're small in number and consistently applied. One real scheme is genuinely different: the US government's Confidential, Secret, and Top Secret system for national security information. Legally defined, its own clearance process — don't confuse it with commercial data classification.

The transferable skill isn't memorizing one vendor's label names — it's recognizing the pattern: a small number of tiers, each with a defined answer for access, consequence, and controls. Next lesson: you can't classify what you haven't found — discovering sensitive data in the first place.
